title: Prescription Opioid Misuse: Signs and Recovery
desc: Learn to recognize prescription opioid misuse, understand dependence, and discover evidence-based treatment options including MAT and medical detox in California.
h1: Prescription Opioid Misuse: Recognizing the Signs and Finding Recovery
author: California Treatment Centers Editorial Team
bodyHtml:
Prescription opioid misuse has become one of the most serious public health challenges in the United States. According to the National Institute on Drug Abuse (NIDA), roughly 9.7 million people reported misusing prescription pain relievers in 2020 alone. Understanding how misuse develops—and what recovery looks like—is the first step toward getting help.

What Is Prescription Opioid Misuse?

Prescription opioids include medications such as oxycodone, hydrocodone, codeine, and morphine. They are prescribed to manage moderate to severe pain, but they also carry a significant risk of dependence and misuse. Misuse means taking a medication in a way other than prescribed—taking a higher dose, using someone else's prescription, or taking the drug to produce a feeling of euphoria rather than to treat pain.

Over time, the brain adapts to the presence of opioids. Tolerance builds, meaning the same dose produces less relief, and physical dependence develops so that stopping or reducing the drug causes withdrawal symptoms. This is a medical process, not a moral failing, and it can happen even to people who take opioids exactly as directed.

Warning Signs of Prescription Opioid Misuse

MedlinePlus, a service of the National Library of Medicine, notes several behavioral and physical signs that may indicate opioid misuse:

  • Taking more of a medication than prescribed or taking it more frequently
  • Running out of a prescription earlier than expected
  • Visiting multiple doctors or pharmacies to obtain additional prescriptions (“doctor shopping”)
  • Mood swings, drowsiness, or confusion that are uncharacteristic
  • Withdrawal-like symptoms—nausea, sweating, anxiety, muscle aches—when the medication is not available
  • Neglecting responsibilities at work, school, or home
  • Social withdrawal or secrecy about medication use

These signs alone do not confirm an opioid use disorder (OUD), but they are important signals that a conversation with a healthcare provider is warranted.

The Link Between Prescription Opioids and Illicit Drug Use

One of the greatest dangers of untreated prescription opioid misuse is escalation. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) reports that people who are dependent on prescription opioids are far more likely to transition to heroin or illicit fentanyl—substances that are dramatically more potent and unpredictable in their street form. Illicitly manufactured fentanyl is now responsible for the vast majority of opioid overdose deaths in the United States.

This trajectory underscores why early intervention is so important. Addressing prescription opioid misuse before it escalates can literally save a life.

Health Risks Beyond Overdose

Overdose is the most acute risk, but chronic opioid misuse damages health in other ways. It suppresses immune function, disrupts hormonal balance, and—particularly with injectable use—increases the risk of infectious disease. Opioid misuse also frequently co-occurs with depression, anxiety, and post-traumatic stress disorder. The National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism (NIAAA) emphasizes that co-occurring mental health conditions must be treated alongside substance use disorders for long-term recovery to be achievable.

Evidence-Based Treatment Options

Recovery from opioid use disorder is absolutely possible. The foundation of treatment for most people involves two phases:

Medical Detox

Opioid withdrawal, while rarely life-threatening on its own, is intensely uncomfortable and is a common reason people return to use. Medical detoxification provides 24/7 clinical monitoring and medications such as buprenorphine or methadone to ease withdrawal symptoms safely. This content is for educational purposes only and is not medical advice. Always consult a qualified healthcare provider before making treatment decisions.

Medication-Assisted Treatment (MAT)

Medication-assisted treatment combines FDA-approved medications with counseling and behavioral therapies. According to the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (SAMHSA), buprenorphine (Suboxone), methadone, and naltrexone (Vivitrol) are the three FDA-approved medications for opioid use disorder. Research consistently shows MAT reduces illicit opioid use, decreases overdose deaths, and improves social functioning. These medications are not simply substituting one addiction for another—they restore neurological balance that allows people to engage meaningfully in therapy and daily life.

Behavioral Therapies and Ongoing Support

Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), motivational interviewing, and contingency management are among the most studied behavioral approaches for OUD. Peer support groups and recovery housing further reinforce the skills learned in formal treatment.

Talking to a Doctor and What to Expect

If you or a loved one is concerned about opioid use, speaking with a primary care provider is a reasonable first step. Clinicians are required to treat substance use disorders with the same confidentiality protections they extend to any other medical condition. You can also locate treatment providers through SAMHSA's National Helpline at 1-800-662-4357 (free, confidential, 24/7) or by calling the 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline if you or someone you know is in immediate danger.

At California Treatment Centers, we work with most major insurers and offer multiple California locations. If you have questions about coverage or care options, we encourage you to reach out at any time.

faq.q: What is the difference between opioid dependence and opioid addiction?
faq.a: Physical dependence means the body has adapted to the drug and withdrawal symptoms occur if it is stopped abruptly—this can happen with legitimate medical use. Opioid use disorder (addiction) involves compulsive use despite harmful consequences. Dependence alone does not mean a person has an addiction, but the two often co-occur. A healthcare provider can help distinguish them and recommend appropriate treatment.

faq.q: Is medication-assisted treatment (MAT) effective for prescription opioid misuse?
faq.a: Yes. According to SAMHSA, FDA-approved medications—buprenorphine, methadone, and naltrexone—significantly reduce opioid use, overdose risk, and criminal activity while improving treatment retention. MAT is most effective when combined with counseling and support services.

faq.q: Will my insurance cover prescription opioid treatment in California?
faq.a: Under the Mental Health Parity and Addiction Equity Act, most insurance plans that cover mental health or substance use treatment must do so on terms comparable to medical or surgical benefits. California Treatment Centers is in-network with most major insurers. Contact us or call your insurer directly to verify your specific benefits.

faq.q: Where can I get immediate help for opioid misuse?
faq.a: Call the SAMHSA National Helpline at 1-800-662-4357 (free, confidential, 24/7) to find local treatment options. If there is an immediate risk of overdose, call 911. For emotional support, the 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline is available around the clock.

title: Exercise and Addiction Recovery: The Science
desc: Regular physical activity can reduce cravings, improve mood, and support brain healing in recovery. Evidence-based guidance for those in California treatment programs.
h1: Exercise and Addiction Recovery: What the Science Says
author: California Treatment Centers Editorial Team
bodyHtml:
Physical activity may be the last thing on someone's mind during early recovery, yet a growing body of research suggests that regular exercise can meaningfully support sobriety and overall wellbeing. This article summarizes the evidence and offers practical guidance. It is general education, not medical advice; always consult your clinical team before starting a new exercise program, especially if you have underlying health conditions.

How Exercise Affects the Brain in Recovery

Substance use disorders alter the brain's reward system — particularly the dopamine circuits that regulate motivation and reinforcement. The National Institute on Drug Abuse (NIDA) explains that the brain can adapt and heal during recovery, though the process takes time and support. Research has found that aerobic exercise increases dopamine and other mood-regulating neurotransmitters, helping to partially restore the brain chemistry disrupted by long-term substance use.

Exercise also stimulates the release of endorphins — the body's natural mood-elevating compounds — and promotes neuroplasticity, the brain's ability to form new, healthier connections. This matters in recovery because building new behavioral patterns requires a brain that is as resilient as possible.

Reducing Cravings and Withdrawal Discomfort

Managing cravings is one of the most challenging aspects of early recovery. MedlinePlus, a service of the National Library of Medicine, summarizes broad benefits of regular physical activity, including improvements in mood, anxiety, and stress tolerance — three of the most common drivers of cravings and relapse risk. Even a brisk 10-minute walk during a craving episode can shift the body's stress response and interrupt the urge before it peaks.

Exercise can also ease post-acute withdrawal syndrome (PAWS) — the lingering fatigue, sleep disruption, and mood instability that persist for weeks or months after acute withdrawal ends. Regular movement tends to improve sleep quality, increase energy levels over time, and help regulate mood, making the early weeks of recovery more manageable.

Mental Health Benefits in Recovery

Depression and anxiety commonly co-occur with substance use disorders, and unaddressed mental health symptoms are a significant relapse risk. The Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (SAMHSA) emphasizes treating the whole person in recovery, including mental health. Aerobic exercise is one of the most consistently supported non-pharmacological approaches for reducing depressive and anxiety symptoms, and the benefits tend to compound with regular practice over weeks.

Social forms of exercise — group fitness classes, recreational leagues, or recovery-focused running groups — carry an additional benefit: community. Isolation is a major relapse risk factor, and activities that build genuine connection offer both structure and belonging during a vulnerable period.

Practical Tips for Getting Started

Beginning an exercise routine in early recovery does not require athletic experience or an expensive gym membership. Some practical starting points:

  • Start small and be consistent. Even 15 to 20 minutes of walking three to four times a week can produce measurable benefits. Consistency matters more than intensity, especially early in recovery.
  • Choose activities you enjoy. Exercise that feels punishing is unlikely to become a lasting habit. Experiment with walking, yoga, cycling, swimming, or strength training to find what resonates.
  • Consult your care team first. If you have health concerns — especially cardiovascular, liver, or musculoskeletal issues related to substance use — check with a medical provider before starting a new program. This is particularly important if you are still in an active treatment setting.
  • Use movement as a complement, not a replacement. Exercise supports recovery but does not substitute for evidence-based care. Medication-assisted treatment, behavioral therapy, and peer support remain the foundation of lasting recovery.
  • Be alert to compulsive patterns. For some individuals, addictive tendencies can shift to behaviors like excessive exercise. If movement starts to feel compulsive or interferes with treatment, raise it with your counselor.

Exercise in Formal Treatment and Aftercare

Many quality treatment programs now integrate physical activity as a component of comprehensive care. Yoga, mindfulness movement, and recreational therapy are common offerings in residential and intensive outpatient settings. These activities provide healthy structure, support stress management, and begin building the habits and routines that sustain recovery long after discharge.

After completing a formal program, staying active is a meaningful part of an aftercare and relapse prevention plan. Building regular movement into a recovery routine provides structure, accountability, and a reliable mood-management tool — one that requires no prescription and belongs entirely to the person in recovery.

Taking the Next Step

Recovery is built one healthy choice at a time, and exercise is one powerful tool among many. For free, confidential treatment referrals available 24 hours a day, call the SAMHSA National Helpline at 1-800-662-4357. If you or someone you love is in crisis, call or text the 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline. California Treatment Centers is in-network with most major insurers and has multiple locations across California. Call 213-321-6518 to speak with our team today. This content is for educational purposes only and does not constitute medical advice.

faq.q: Can exercise really help with addiction recovery?
faq.a: Research suggests that regular physical activity can support recovery by reducing cravings, improving mood, and promoting brain healing. It is a valuable complement to evidence-based treatment — not a replacement. Always discuss any new exercise program with your clinical team. This is general education, not medical advice.

faq.q: What type of exercise is best for someone in recovery?
faq.a: There is no single best type. Any consistent movement you enjoy is likely to be beneficial. Walking, swimming, yoga, cycling, and strength training are all options. The most important factor is regularity and finding an activity that you can sustain over time.

faq.q: Is it safe to exercise during early recovery?
faq.a: For most people, light to moderate exercise is safe and beneficial during early recovery, but the right answer depends on your individual health history. Talk with your doctor or treatment team before starting a new exercise program, especially if you have cardiovascular or other health concerns related to substance use.

faq.q: Does California Treatment Centers offer fitness or activity programming?
faq.a: Many quality treatment programs, including those in our network, incorporate physical activity, yoga, or recreational therapy as part of comprehensive care. Call us at 213-321-6518 to learn more about program offerings and whether we are in-network with your insurance.
